entry.coreIdea: A cause label attached to the result.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Logical phrase introducing a cause: staff illness explains why the meeting was postponed.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: the phrase identifies a reason without itself expressing blame.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Matter-of-fact here: the sentence reports the postponement and its cause without a distinctive emotional attitude.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Relatively formal, common in notices and reports. “Because of” sounds more ordinary in conversation.

when_to_use: Write a short postponement notice explaining staff absence. A model in this sense: The match was cancelled owing to heavy rain.
when_not_to_use: Owing to takes a noun phrase; because takes a clause.
It sounds more formal than because of and is common in notices.

advanced_nuance: owing to: It sounds more formal than because of and is common in notices.

memory_practice.memory_sentence: The match was cancelled owing to heavy rain.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a short postponement notice explaining staff absence. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: because of a particular cause. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which option fits the taught meaning and standard construction? A: Owing to heavy rain, we cancelled. B: Owing to it rained, we cancelled. Explain your choice, then check the correction and distinction.

meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: A cause label attached to the result. Owing to takes a noun phrase; because takes a clause.

mistakes_differences.important_difference: Owing to takes a noun phrase; because takes a clause.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: peer-ee-OD-ik-lee. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.coreIdea: An action happens again after gaps in time.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Time adverb meaning at intervals; here, predictions are run repeatedly on batches rather than necessarily continuously.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it describes timing, not whether the frequency is sufficient.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Technical and factual here: the sentence explains how the prediction process is scheduled.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral to formal; common in operational descriptions. “From time to time” is less precise and more conversational.

when_to_use: Use periodically for an action that is repeated with gaps between occasions.
It suits maintenance checks, reviews and scheduled processing.
when_not_to_use: Do not use periodically to mean continuously without a break.
Give an exact interval, such as every hour, if the reader needs a precise schedule.

advanced_nuance: Periodically does not by itself specify the length or exact regularity of the gaps; add a schedule when precision matters.
Periodically describes timing, not how carefully or successfully the task is performed.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture repeated check marks with spaces between them on a timeline.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: We check the supplies periodically and order more when needed.
memory_practice.recall_question: What separates periodic checks from continuous monitoring?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which is periodic? A: A check at several separate times. B: Watching every moment without stopping. Explain the gaps.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a maintenance note for a colleague. Use periodically and give a concrete interval for a fictional equipment check.

examples.example_1: We periodically review the contact list to remove outdated numbers.
examples.example_2: The caretaker checks the empty building periodically during the winter.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Is someone watching the equipment all day?
B: No, we check it periodically, once every two hours.
A: Please record each check in the log.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Predictions are run periodically on a batch of inputs.
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Predictions are made on groups of inputs at repeated times, rather than being described as one continuous operation.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “The list is updated periodic.” The verb needs the adverb periodically.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “The list is updated periodically.” Use periodic before a noun, as in “periodic updates.”
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Periodically means repeatedly with intervals. Continuously means without interruption.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: periodically + verb; verb + periodically; be + periodically + past participle

semanticReview.finding: Adverb position and periodic/periodically distinction checked. No technical correctness inferred from timing.

entry.englishMeaning: to do extra work because someone or something is not doing enough
entry.coreIdea: Pull a loose rope tight by taking the extra load.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative idiom: take on work left undone by others, as though taking up looseness in a rope.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Can suggest helpful cooperation or an unfair extra burden; here, colleagues cover temporary absences.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Practical and cooperative here: the evening team is described as covering work while two people are away.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Conversational, including ordinary workplace discussions. “Cover the extra work” is more direct in a formal allocation plan.

when_to_use: Use “pick up the slack” for this meaning: to do extra work because someone or something is not doing enough. For a concrete situation: The evening team will pick up the slack while two colleagues are away.
when_not_to_use: Pick up the slack means compensate for a shortfall in effort or capacity; help out does not necessarily imply anyone is falling short.

advanced_nuance: pick up the slack: The phrase may sound accusatory, so distinguish planned cover from blaming an absent colleague.

memory_practice.production_task: Use “pick up the slack” in your own response: Ask for temporary cover during an absence without unfairly criticising the absent person.

memory_practice.recognition_task: Compare these two statements and choose the accurate form or interpretation. A: “We need someone to pick up the slack.” B: “We need someone to pick the slack.” Explain the difference before checking Mistakes & Differences.

entry.englishMeaning: to decide that a possibility cannot or should not be considered
entry.coreIdea: Cross an option off the list.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract phrasal verb meaning to exclude a possibility; in the negative, a further delay remains possible.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it expresses an assessment rather than approval or dislike of the possibility.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Cautious here: “cannot” and “at this stage” avoid giving an assurance that there will be no delay.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and widely used in discussion, reports and news. It does not mean that the remaining possibility is certain or likely.

when_to_use: Use “rule out” for this meaning: to decide that a possibility cannot or should not be considered. For a concrete situation: We cannot rule out a further delay at this stage.
when_not_to_use: Rule out removes an option from consideration; postpone keeps it possible for later.

advanced_nuance: rule out: Cannot rule out means something remains possible, not that it is likely or certain.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Cross an option off the list.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The forecast does not rule out rain later in the day.
memory_practice.production_task: Use “rule out” in your own response: Explain why you cannot exclude a further delay without predicting that it will happen.
memory_practice.recall_question: Without looking at the heading, recall the expression meaning “to decide that a possibility cannot or should not be considered”. Then explain it in your own words.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Compare these two statements and choose the accurate form or interpretation. A: “We ruled out to postpone the event.” B: “We ruled out postponing the event.” Explain the difference before checking Mistakes & Differences.

examples.workplace: We cannot rule out a further delay at this stage.
examples.another_context: The forecast does not rule out rain later in the day.

B: Then we should keep a backup date available.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We cannot rule out a further delay at this stage.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to decide that a possibility cannot or should not be considered
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Cross an option off the list. Here, to decide that a possibility cannot or should not be considered.

mistakes_differences.correction: We ruled out postponing the event.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: We ruled out to postpone the event.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Rule out removes an option from consideration; postpone keeps it possible for later.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: TERR-er. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: an intense or overwhelming feeling of fear
entry.coreIdea: Fear so strong that it feels overwhelming.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract noun for extremely strong fear; here, it describes how frightened Kevin's colleagues appeared.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Strongly negative as an emotional experience; it is much more intense than mild concern.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Dramatic here: the contrast between their apparent terror and Kevin continuing heightens the tension.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in vivid narrative and serious accounts of fear. It may overstate ordinary workplace nervousness.

when_to_use: Use terror for an extremely strong feeling of fear.
It can describe a frightening experience or intense fear about what might happen.
when_not_to_use: For mild concern about a small problem, worry or nervousness is usually more accurate.
Do not assume the person's fear proves that the danger is objectively as great as it feels.

advanced_nuance: Terror names the feeling, while the source's apparent limits the claim to how the colleagues look.
In this emotional sense, terror is normally uncountable: 'filled with terror' or 'a feeling of terror'.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a frightened character unable to move for a moment.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: She stood in terror as the locked door slowly opened.
memory_practice.recall_question: Is terror normally stronger or weaker than ordinary nervousness?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which best fits terror? A: Slight concern about a late bus. B: Overwhelming fear during a frightening escape. Explain the degree of fear.
memory_practice.production_task: Write two sentences about a fictional suspense scene. Use terror to describe a character's intense fear without drawing on a personal experience.

examples.example_1: She froze in terror when she heard footsteps inside the empty house.
examples.example_2: The boy's face showed sheer terror as the dog charged toward him.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Why did the character stop moving?
B: She was frozen with terror when she saw the figure at the window.
A: So she was too frightened to act.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: But  Kevin  ignored  the  apparent  terror  of  his  col­ leagues  and  plunged  on  ahead.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: an intense or overwhelming feeling of fear
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Kevin's colleagues appear extremely afraid, but he continues. Apparent signals how their reaction looks; the excerpt does not say exactly what each person feels.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “He was terror.” Terror is the noun naming the feeling.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “He felt terror” or “He was terrified.” Terror names the feeling; terrified describes the person.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Fear covers a broad range of intensity. Terror stresses an extreme, overwhelming degree.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: feel terror; in terror; be filled with terror; terror at + frightening event

semanticReview.finding: Extreme emotional fear only; source apparent preserved, noun/adjective distinction and fictional practice checked.
